issues.legal_issue: A valid execution sale to a stranger purchaser must be confirmed even when the decree is set aside after the sale but before confirmation, unless a recognized ground prevents confirmation or the sale is successfully set aside through the prescribed process.
material_facts: An ex parte money decree existed when the judgment-debtor’s house was sold in execution, and a person who was a stranger to the suit became the highest bidder.
After the sale, the judgment-debtor applied to set aside the ex parte decree, which was set aside before the sale was confirmed.

The judgment-debtor also objected to the sale, alleging undervaluation and defects in publication and timing, but did not obtain an order setting aside the sale; the alleged collusion with the decree-holder was not substantiated.
The execution court confirmed the sale, and the Supreme Court held that the purchaser was entitled to confirmation despite the later setting aside of the decree.
issues.conclusion: The sale had to be confirmed: setting aside the decree after a valid sale did not, by itself, prevent confirmation in favour of a stranger purchaser.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXI, rules 89–91 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the judgment-debtor or purchaser may seek to set aside an execution sale on the specified grounds; under rule 92, where no such application is made or it is disallowed, the court must confirm the sale. Section 65 provides that, once the sale becomes absolute, the purchaser’s title relates back to the date of sale. The 1908 Code contains no provision making confirmation unavailable merely because the underlying decree is later reversed or set aside. The Court relied on Nanhelal v. Umrao Singh, which held that an execution sale duly carried out and involving a third-party interest could not be disregarded outside the prescribed process; Sorimuthu v. Muthukrishna and Birdichand v. Ganpatsao, which supported confirmation after reversal of the decree absent a successful application to set aside the sale; and the policy, also reflected in Amhujammal v. Thangavelu Chettiar and S. Chokalingam v. N. S. Krishna, of protecting an innocent stranger purchaser so that execution sales attract bidders. The Court recognized exceptional cases, including a sale held without notice to the judgment-debtor, a court misled in fixing the reserve price, or a sale held when no decree existed.

rule.if: execution_sale_confirmation and sale_valid_when_held and decree_existed_when_sale_held and stranger_purchaser and no_successful_sale_challenge and no_exceptional_confirmation_bar

predicates.execution_sale_confirmation: The proceeding concerns whether a court should confirm property sold in execution of a decree.
predicates.sale_valid_when_held: The sale was duly held under an existing execution process and was not invalid for a defect that prevents confirmation.
predicates.decree_existed_when_sale_held: A decree authorizing execution existed when the property was sold.
predicates.stranger_purchaser: The purchaser was not a party to the suit and was not the decree-holder purchasing the property.
predicates.no_successful_sale_challenge: The judgment-debtor or purchaser did not obtain an order setting aside the sale through a challenge to it.
predicates.no_exceptional_confirmation_bar: The sale was not held without required notice, was not affected by the court being misled in fixing a reserve price, and was not held when no decree existed.
predicates.sale_confirmed_despite_later_decree_set_: The sale is confirmed even though the decree is set aside after the sale.

issues.definition: When a valid execution sale made under an existing decree is to be confirmed, a stranger purchaser is protected if no challenge succeeds and no exceptional bar applies, so the sale is confirmed despite the decree later being set aside.
